## Overview
<!--
At a high-level address what your proposal is and how it will address
the problem identified. Highlight any benefits to the R Community that
follow from solving the problem. This should be your most compelling
section.

Include concrete actions you will take and estimated timeline.
-->

This proposal outlines a documentation linting tool in the form of an R package which wraps Vale, so that it can be run from R, on the command line and on CI, together with a Vale style written for R package documentation.

It provides instant feedback on documentation quality, enabling both humans and AI tools to produce better quality documentation that will be clear and easy to understand for end users.

The tool lints key user-facing package documentation: code comments in R source files, package vignettes, package READMEs and NEWS files.

The applied rules are configurable by the end user, according to taste, with the defaults reflecting established advice on writing for users, drawing on the conventions built into existing Vale styles such as those for the Google and Microsoft developer documentation style guides.

The project will deliver the R package, the style, a GitHub Action and the first set of rules between January and April 2027, with later milestones adding a pre-commit hook and AGENTS.md support.

## Detail
<!--
Go into more detail about the specifics of the project and how it delivers
against the problem.

Depending on project type the detail section should include:
-->

### Minimum Viable Product

The MVP for this project is a small R package which installs Vale, runs it over a package, and returns a list of lints, including the file name, line number, the rule which was violated, and a message explaining what was wrong. The output will be a data frame in R and human-readable text on the command line, with an option to output in JSON for AI tools and CI reporting.

The MVP will cover documentation in R code comments, package vignettes, and any README present in the repository.

As the intention is that users can use this tool on CI, the MVP will also include a GitHub Action to run it.

In terms of rules applied to the text, Vale already provides rules for sentence length, readability scores, and use of words often reported by readers as condescending like "simply", "just", "easy", "obviously", and "clearly", spread across several existing styles with thresholds tuned for general prose. The work in the MVP is to select the subset of these rules that make sense for R package documentation, set their thresholds so that they aren't noisy on real packages, and add a vocabulary of common R terms so that these aren't reported as errors. Together these form the default style that ships with the package. The rules will be configurable via a Vale config file in the package root directory, which the package can generate with sensible defaults.

Once the MVP exists, adding rules that don't already exist in Vale and other sources of text such as NEWS files is incremental work. Later milestones include adding a pre-commit hook and a command that writes the active rules into a project's AGENTS.md.

### Architecture

The tool will be written in R and Vale's YAML rule format, and will have 3 main components:

1 - the binary - the package will find an existing Vale installation, or download the Vale binary for the user's platform from Vale's GitHub Releases when the user asks it to, following the pattern used by packages such as tinytex and pandoc. Vale handles extracting comments from R files and parsing Markdown.

2 - the style - a Vale style, which is a directory of rules defined as data rather than code, together with a vocabulary of R terms. This is published so that it can also be used by people who run Vale directly, without the R package.

3 - the R interface, config, and tests - functions to generate a config file at the package root, run Vale, and return the results as a data frame, along with the GitHub Action. Rules are configured from the config file and each has its own tests.

### Assumptions

<!--
What assumptions are you making that, if proven false, would invalidate the project?
-->

Assumptions and ideas for mitigation are as follows:

- Vale continues to be maintained and its support for extracting comments from R files remains adequate. Vale is actively developed, and has a stable release process with binaries for all major platforms.
- Useful prose rules don't need heavy NLP. Sentence splitting, syllable counting and word lists are enough for the rules in scope, including readability scores, as Vale shows.
- Sensible defaults can be found empirically. Work on docreview showed that readability scores are sensitive to text length, and a threshold that works for a vignette is wrong for a short code comment. Rather than guessing, the defaults and any minimum text length for a rule to apply will be set by running the tool over real packages and looking at the distribution of scores, so that the rules aren't noisy out of the box.
- Building on Vale keeps the amount of novel code small. Confirming that Vale can be installed and run from R on all platforms is the first milestone, so that this is proven before the rule work starts.

### External dependencies

<!--
What external dependencies does the project have (e.g. libraries, services, other projects, etc.)?
-->

- Vale, installed as a binary from its GitHub Releases.
- Existing Vale style packages, such as Readability, as a starting point for rules.
- GitHub Actions for CI and releases.

Nothing requires a service or a paid account, so there are no ongoing costs.
